title: What We Can Learn from the Anti-Microbial Properties of Insect Wings
content: Candida albicans is a ubiquitous yeast found on the skin of most humans as well as in the human digestive and urinary tracts. Normally, the presence of Candida is symptomless and benign. However, Candida can form biofilms that increase their virulence potential [1]. Yeast biofilm formation occurs when the yeast cells attach to a surface, rapidly divide, transition into a filamentous form (hyphae), and secrete extracellular materials (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids), which encase the cells and form a complex three-dimensional structure. Becoming encased within the biofilm makes Candida significantly more resistant to antifungal drugs. Yeasts are able to form biofilms on biological surfaces but also on abiotic surfaces like those of medical devices such as catheters and prosthetics. Candidiasis (Candida infection) is a significant health problem. It is estimated to be a contributing factor in 15–35% of adult hospital deaths and 10–15% of newborn mortalities [2]. Since biofilm formation is a key aspect of Candida drug resistance, methods to prevent or reduce biofilm formation could aid in the treatment of Candida infections.
